title: The impact understanding of exosome therapy in COVID-19 and preparations for the future approaches in dealing with infec

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Conclusions versus Results/experimental description
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states that five ICU patients were “subjected to both inactivated SARS-CoV-2 and exosome therapy” and concludes that “exosome administration” is safe and efficacious. The Results clarify that only PBMCs isolated from five patients and five controls were exposed in vitro to inactivated virus and exosomes. No patient received exosomes, and no clinical treatment, safety, or efficacy outcome was measured. The abstract and conclusion therefore misrepresent an in-vitro PBMC experiment as patient therapy.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract final sentences; Discussion opening and Conclusions
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims that the findings “underscore the potential safety and efficacy of exosomes as a therapeutic strategy for COVID-19” and that administering exosomes is beneficial for patients with COVID-19 hyperinflammation. An ex-vivo cytokine assay with PBMCs from five patients cannot establish clinical safety, therapeutic efficacy, antiviral efficacy, dose safety, or patient benefit. No participants were administered exosomes and no adverse-event or clinical endpoint data are reported.

Table 4 is titled “Comparing cytokine levels after exosome treatment using paired T-test” and its caption defines SD, 95% CI, t statistic, and Cohen’s d. However, every displayed analysis is reported as a median ± IQR with a Z statistic and an r effect size, which are Wilcoxon signed-rank reporting conventions rather than paired-t-test conventions. The title/caption and the actual statistics are mutually inconsistent; the correct test and effect-size method must be identified and the table corrected.

Table 5 states that the Wilcoxon effect size is calculated as r = Z/√N and that n = 5. For the repeated reported value Z = -2.023, this formula with N=5 gives |r| = 2.023/√5 = 0.905, not the reported 0.64. The reported 0.64 instead equals 2.023/√10, contradicting the stated sample size and formula. Thus the reported effect sizes are incorrectly calculated or incorrectly documented.

The manuscript performs numerous unadjusted hypothesis tests across four cytokines, two groups, four experimental conditions, and multiple before/after comparisons, repeatedly treating P<0.05 as significant. No multiplicity correction or prespecified primary endpoint is described. The repeatedly reported P=0.043 results would not remain significant under standard family-wise correction even within the four-cytokine family. Statements that all or most observed cytokine changes are significant require corrected analyses or explicit exploratory qualification.

The manuscript states that doses of 10, 20, 40, and 60 µg/mL were evaluated, then says that “a dose of 40 µg/mL (the highest dose) was selected.” This is numerically false because 60 µg/mL is the highest listed dose. The dose-selection statement must be corrected and a scientifically justified reason supplied if 40 rather than 60 µg/mL was selected.

The authors state: “Infection with SARS-CoV-2 resulted in the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.” The experiment exposed PBMC cultures to inactivated SARS-CoV-2 for 24 h; it did not demonstrate PBMC infection, viral replication, or productive infection. Inactivated-virus stimulation can trigger cytokine release without infection. The statement must be changed to describe stimulation/exposure rather than infection unless infection is independently demonstrated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph beginning “Human umbilical cord-derived (hUC-MSCs) are the primary source of MSCs”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The categorical assertion that hUC-MSCs “are the primary source of MSCs” is factually misleading. MSCs are isolated from multiple established sources, including bone marrow, adipose tissue, umbilical cord/Wharton’s jelly, placenta, and dental tissues; hUC-MSCs are an important source but not universally the primary source. This should be qualified and supported with an appropriate source-specific statement.

The paper presents exosomes as inherently “non-toxic,” “low immunogenicity (lacking MHC class I–II),” and suitable as readily available therapeutic products. These are not universal intrinsic properties of all exosomes/MSC extracellular-vesicle preparations: cargo, co-isolated contaminants, dose, route, and parent-cell source affect toxicity and immunogenicity, and extracellular vesicles can contain MHC molecules. The unqualified statements overstate the evidence and are especially problematic given the paper’s later safety claim.
